------------------------------------------------
           RESEARCH UNIT FOR WILDLIFE POPULATION ASSESSMENT
                 INTERNATIONAL TRAINING WORKSHOPS 2000
           ------------------------------------------------

                   Introduction to Distance Sampling
                           August 28 - 30

    Advanced Techniques and Recent Developments in Distance Sampling
                       August 31 - September 2

            University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland

            -----------------------------------------------
            http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distanceworkshop/
            -----------------------------------------------

Overview
--------

Distance sampling is the most widely used method for estimating the abundance
of wildlife populations. The aim of these workshops is to train participants
in the latest methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys,
including line and point transects.  The workshops are taught by leading
researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop will run at an introductory level, and will focus on
"conventional" distance sampling methods, as described in the standard
reference book Distance Sampling.  The workshop will be a blend of theory and
practice and participants will learn how to use the program Distance (version
3.5).  Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and
methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.

The second workshop will cover the latest advances in distance sampling
research and software. It is intended for those already familiar with
conventional distance sampling methods.  Participants will learn the use of
covariates for modelling the detection function, double-platform methods for
when g(0) < 1, spatial modelling of density, automated survey design and
adaptive sampling.  Computer sessions will use a preliminary version of the
new software Distance 4.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets,
and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.

Instructors
-----------

The workshop instructors are Prof. Stephen Buckland, Dr. David Borchers and
Dr. Len Thomas.  All three are at the forefront of research into distance
sampling methods, and development of software to apply the new methods. They
have extensive experience teaching distance sampling, including previous
highly successful workshops taught in the UK, USA, Norway, and New Zealand.

Cost
----

The course fees are 440 UK pounds for one workshop and 745 pounds for both
workshops, with a 25% discount for registered students.  For registrations
received after June 30th, a late-registration supplement of 50 pounds will
apply.  The fee covers tuition, all course materials and refreshments at
morning and afternoon breaks.  The number of places is limited to 30 on the
first workshop and 18 on the second, and will be filled on a first-come
first-served basis.

Further information
-------------------

The workshop booklet is on the world-wide web at
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distanceworkshop/

Registration forms are available at that site.

If you would like a printed copy of this information or have any
questions about the workshops, please contact

The = Cumbria Bird Club is currently nearing the end of a Breeding Birds = Survey which has included collection of relative abundance and = distribution data. As part of this, we are also looking to calculate = population estimates. =20 We have chosen point counts as our preferred method of data collection - = this should allow us to be more precise when it comes to looking at = different habitats. He is then to record the habitat = (using the BTO's BBS habitat recording codes). After allowing 5 minutes = for the birds to settle, the observer is to spend 10 minutes recording = each bird seen/heard within 4 bands: (0-10m; 10-25m; 25-100m; >100m). =20 Having trialled the methodology over the past few days, I have the = following problems: =20 1. Much of Cumbria is farmland (50% or more). Many of the bird species = found in this habitat favour field edges such as hedges. Their = distribution is therefore not even. Anyone standing more than 100m from = the hedge will pick up the majority of the birds in the band (> 100m). = Similarly if one is right next to the hedge, the bulk of the birds will = be in the bands 0-10m and 10-25m. I personally cannot think of a = practical way around this. I suspect it also creates analytical = problems. Do you have any practical suggestions. =20 2. Detectability. In the majority of passerine species, the male is more = obvious than the female during the breeding season.Should we be = recording different sexes where possible? Should we ignore females for = species where we can separate sexes? Does the program "Distance" allow a = correction? =20 3. Analysis. We are planning two visits to each point - one in late = April/early May, the second late May/early June. Some resident species = are more detectable early on in the breeding season. In fact, I am aware = that in the space of a week, species like Marsh Tit can go from being = easy to count to difficult to find. =20 Bearing this in mind, how should we proceed with the final analysis - = should we take the higher of the two counts as our estimate or should we = use both counts? I do not believe that the two counts are independant, = but would welcome some suggestions. =20 Banding - for an open habitat such as farmland, I suspect we may have to = lump together the habitat in the two closest bands and do a separate = analysis. messages.body_plain:
> > The observer will be told what habitat he is being asked to sample in
> > the square and to go the centre of the 1 km square and find the nearest
> > piece of uniform habitat (>100mx100m). He is then to record the habitat
> > (using the BTO's BBS habitat recording codes). After allowing 5 minutes
> > for the birds to settle, the observer is to spend 10 minutes recording
> > each bird seen/heard within 4 bands: (0-10m; 10-25m; 25-100m; >100m).

There are a few problems with this methodology.  Firstly, selecting the
nearest bit of uniform habitat negates the random design.  It will for
example bias against species found mostly in mixed habitat.  Far better
either to sample at the centre of each sampled square, and record habitat
category/categories within say 25m of the point, allowing you to
post-stratify analysis by habitat, or use your available data to stratify
by habitat in advance, and sample km squares from each habitat
classification.  Also, counting for 10mins at each point will be
disastrous if you really want to estimate absolute numbers.  Bird movement
will give you estimates of density an order of magnitude too high for some
species.  Many surveys use this approach, and many of those have generated
very biased density estimates.  The bias can be eliminated by doing a
'snapshot' count.  Take a few minutes at the start, to determine what
birds are where, and of which species.  Set your watch say to beep after
perhaps 5mins;  that is your snapshot moment.  Take a few more minutes to
confirm locations and identification of birds that were present at the
snapshot moment.  If you really don't know where a bird was at that
moment, don't record a distance band for it - and exclude it from the
point transect analysis.

> > Having trialled the methodology over the past few days, I have the
> > following problems:
> >
> > 1. Much of Cumbria is farmland (50% or more). Many of the bird species
> > found in this habitat favour field edges such as hedges. Their
> > distribution is therefore not even. Anyone standing more than 100m from
> > the hedge will pick up the majority of the birds in the band (>
> > 100m). Similarly if one is right next to the hedge, the bulk of the
> > birds will be in the bands 0-10m and 10-25m. I personally cannot think
> > of a practical way around this. I suspect it also creates analytical
> > problems. Do you have any practical suggestions.

This is why it is critical that you do NOT instruct observers to locate a
patch of uniform habitat.  The sample points should be random with respect
to the habitat, so the birds don't need to be.  The problems you raise
then go away - points close to a hedge are balanced on average by points
further from a hedge, and distribution of birds, ON AVERAGE, is uniform
with respect to distance from a point in any given direction.

> > 2. Detectability. In the majority of passerine species, the male is
> > more obvious than the female during the breeding season.Should we be
> > recording different sexes where possible? Should we ignore females for
> > species where we can separate sexes? Does the program "Distance" allow a
> > correction?

For such species, analyse data for singing individuals.  If you can assume
that this corresponds closely with adult males, and that there is roughly
one adult female per adult male, the (adult) abundance is then double your
estimate.  If it makes more sense for a given species to record sex of
each individual, you can then stratify by sex, rather than by whether the
bird was singing.  You can, in a separate analysis, estimate the
female/non-singing data, if you have sufficient data;  that gives a check
of whether doubling your male estimate is reasonable.

> > 3. Analysis. We are planning two visits to each point - one in late
> > April/early May, the second late May/early June. Some resident species
> > are more detectable early on in the breeding season. In fact, I am aware
> > that in the space of a week, species like Marsh Tit can go from being
> > easy to count to difficult to find.
> >
> > Bearing this in mind, how should we proceed with the final analysis -
> > should we take the higher of the two counts as our estimate or should we
> > use both counts? I do not believe that the two counts are independant,
> > but would welcome some suggestions.

The higher of the 2 counts will again lead you to overestimate
abundance.  For resident species that establish territory early, I would
use the early count only.  For migrant species, I would use the late count
only.  For intermediate species, I might analyse both the early counts and
the late counts in separate analyses, and if not significantly different,
perhaps average the two estimates, to give higher precision.  This can be
done in Distance by stratifying the data by count date - early or late.

> > Banding - for an open habitat such as farmland, I suspect we may have
> > to lump together the habitat in the two closest bands and do a separate
> > analysis. For closed habitats such as woodland, the 10m band is likely
> > to have a reasonable number of birds in. In addition, visibility beyond
> > 25m is limited. Are we going to run into statstical problems if we lump
> > data together and do analyses for different habitats?

Lumping is not a problem, except that you are left with uncomfortably few
intervals for fitting and testing models.  With 3 intervals, you can
either fit a one parameter model and have 1df left for testing model fit,
or fit a 2-parameter model, with no simple option for testing model fit.
I would have been inclined either to push your intervals out a bit - say
15m, 30m, 100m, or add at least one interval - say 10m, 25m, 75m, 150m.  I
would also consider whether it is feasible to issue observers with
Bushnell binocs with laser rangefinders - in which case, allocation to
a larger number of intervals would be much easier.  You should also
consider a training session with observers, to ensure that they can
estimate distance categories well.

Chris Sharpe on the Isle of Man is carrying out similar surveys as part of
their bird atlas, and has addressed many of these issues.

Steve Buckland

> > recording different sexes where possible? Should we ignore females for
> > species where we can separate sexes? Does the program "Distance" allow a
> > correction?

For such species, analyse data for singing individuals.  If you can assume
that this corresponds closely with adult males, and that there is roughly
one adult female per adult male, the (adult) abundance is then double your
estimate.  If it makes more sense for a given species to record sex of
each individual, you can then stratify by sex, rather than by whether the
bird was singing.  You can, in a separate analysis, estimate the
female/non-singing data, if you have sufficient data;  that gives a check
of whether doubling your male estimate is reasonable.

> > 3. Analysis. We are planning two visits to each point - one in late
> > April/early May, the second late May/early June. Some resident species
> > are more detectable early on in the breeding season. In fact, I am aware
> > that in the space of a week, species like Marsh Tit can go from being
> > easy to count to difficult to find.
> >
> > Bearing this in mind, how should we proceed with the final analysis -
> > should we take the higher of the two counts as our estimate or should we
> > use both counts? I do not believe that the two counts are independant,
> > but would welcome some suggestions.

The higher of the 2 counts will again lead you to overestimate
abundance.  For resident species that establish territory early, I would
use the early count only.  For migrant species, I would use the late count
only.  For intermediate species, I might analyse both the early counts and
the late counts in separate analyses, and if not significantly different,
perhaps average the two estimates, to give higher precision.  This can be
done in Distance by stratifying the data by count date - early or late.

> > Banding - for an open habitat such as farmland, I suspect we may have
> > to lump together the habitat in the two closest bands and do a separate
> > analysis. For closed habitats such as woodland, the 10m band is likely
> > to have a reasonable number of birds in. In addition, visibility beyond
> > 25m is limited. Are we going to run into statstical problems if we lump
> > data together and do analyses for different habitats?

Lumping is not a problem, except that you are left with uncomfortably few
intervals for fitting and testing models.  With 3 intervals, you can
either fit a one parameter model and have 1df left for testing model fit,
or fit a 2-parameter model, with no simple option for testing model fit.
I would have been inclined either to push your intervals out a bit - say
15m, 30m, 100m, or add at least one interval - say 10m, 25m, 75m, 150m.  I
would also consider whether it is feasible to issue observers with
Bushnell binocs with laser rangefinders - in which case, allocation to
a larger number of intervals would be much easier.  You should also
consider a training session with observers, to ensure that they can
estimate distance categories well.

Chris Sharpe on the Isle of Man is carrying out similar surveys as part of
their bird atlas, and has addressed many of these issues.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
This is a multi-part message in MIME format.
--------------20CC806E6FA1295D5ABA4FC8
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit

Dear all,
In Cyprus we have an endemic species of wild sheep, the Cyprus mouflon
(Ovis gmelini ophion) that lives in the Paphos forest.  This forest (~
60000 ha) is in the SW part of the island.  The mouflon used to be very
abundant in the middle ages but due to intensive hunting it had reached
the brings of extinction in the 1930s.  Since then it is strictly
protected and the population has reached good numbers, estimated in a
few thousands.  In 1992 a brief helicopter survey was conducted and the
ppln was estimated between 900-1500 animals.  The growing damages that
the mouflon is causing in row crops, vineyards and orchards in areas
near the forest edge has led to the decision in counting the ppln in a
more accurate manner so that the right management decisions could be
taken.  In 1997 the Game Fund, the service responsible for wildlife
conservation in Cyprus has started a program counting the sheep.  We
have established 14 routes (lightly traveled forest roads) that run
through the mouflon habitat and cover most of the forest's valleys.
Every route was traveled at least 2 times, some 3 times by the same
observers between September and January.   We have a 3-year data set
that we started analyzing using DISTANCE.
PROBLEMS:
1.  We plotted the frequency distribution of the right-angle distances
to get the probability density function.  The program chose the
half-normal-cosine model that gave us a ppln estimate of 3600 animals
with a 33% CV!!  Then, we tried the uniform distribution with similar
ppln estimate but with a 22% CV.  We want to try to use the Fourier
Series model but the program does not allow to do so.  Also, it seems
that we cannot use our replications of each route in the program.
Finally, once we put the data in we cannot edit anything in the AREA,
REGION section.
2.  Our observation show that most of the mouflon live in areas close to
the forest edge where food is of a better quality and quantity, thus and
the damage to the crops.  During our analysis we haven't stratified our
routes, ie forest edge habitat and main forest habitat.  We have taken
the entire forest as one study area and may be that's why we get such a
high CV?  Due to the editing problem mentioned in 1. we cannot stratify
our data w/o starting from the beginning.
3.  We are not experienced in this large program that's why we are
sending you our data set for the 1998-1999 count (attachment file) so
you can comment on our work and identify our flaws.  Thanks in advance.

Sincerely yours

Kostas Papageorgiou

Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii

Dear all,
In Cyprus we have an endemic species of wild sheep, the Cyprus mouflon
(Ovis gmelini ophion) that lives in the Paphos forest.  This forest (~
60000 ha) is in the SW part of the island.  The mouflon used to be very
abundant in the middle ages but due to intensive hunting it had reached
the brings of extinction in the 1930s.  Since then it is strictly
protected and the population has reached good numbers, estimated in a
few thousands.  In 1992 a brief helicopter survey was conducted and the
ppln was estimated between 900-1500 animals.  The growing damages that
the mouflon is causing in row crops, vineyards and orchards in areas
near the forest edge has led to the decision in counting the ppln in a
more accurate manner so that the right management decisions could be
taken.  In 1997 the Game Fund, the service responsible for wildlife
conservation in Cyprus has started a program counting the sheep.  We
have established 14 routes (lightly traveled forest roads) that run
through the mouflon habitat and cover most of the forest's valleys.
Every route was traveled at least 2 times, some 3 times by the same
observers between September and January.   We have a 3-year data set
that we started analyzing using DISTANCE.
PROBLEMS:
1.  We plotted the frequency distribution of the right-angle distances
to get the probability density function.  The program chose the
half-normal-cosine model that gave us a ppln estimate of 3600 animals
with a 33% CV!!  Then, we tried the uniform distribution with similar
ppln estimate but with a 22% CV.  We want to try to use the Fourier
Series model but the program does not allow to do so.  Also, it seems
that we cannot use our replications of each route in the program.
Finally, once we put the data in we cannot edit anything in the AREA,
REGION section.
2.  Our observation show that most of the mouflon live in areas close to
the forest edge where food is of a better quality and quantity, thus and
the damage to the crops.  During our analysis we haven't stratified our
routes, ie forest edge habitat and main forest habitat.  We have taken
the entire forest as one study area and may be that's why we get such a
high CV?  Due to the editing problem mentioned in 1. we cannot stratify
our data w/o starting from the beginning.
3.  We are not experienced in this large program that's why we are
sending you our data set for the 1998-1999 count (attachment file) so
you can comment on our work and identify our flaws.  Thanks in advance.

Sincerely yours

Kostas Papageorgiou

messages.subject: Grad Student Needs Work
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am a Master's degree candidate in avian ecology with reasonable
statistical and computer skills.  I have been watching several sites for
some time but have found very few job postings that are year round or
emphasize analytical skills.  I have experience with normal and non-normal
distributions and a variety of statistical packages, though I have as yet no
experience with Distance Sampling.  I have acted as Principal Investigator
on two projects,  assisted on others and presented at several conferences.
I am perfectly happy to assist on ongoing projects.  Ideally, I would prefer
to work near Boston, MA and to start in September, but I am willing to
relocate and am equally flexible as to start date.  I can work at your site
or I can work from home where I have copies of several Statistics Packages.
I have an online resume and list of references available which I can send
you on request.

Thanks in advance for any help you can give.  I would be interested in your
thoughts on this as well as in any leads you may have.

Eric Holt
e-mail: nfi...@massed.net
Note: As I share this e-mail address messages are listed as coming from N.
Fiske.  They are however from me.

messages.subject: ADMIN: No attachments
messages.body_plain:
Could I remind everyone on the distance-sampling list to please refrain from
enclosing attachments with their messages.  This is standard netiquette, and
is also outlined in the list guidelines, which are sent to all new members
when they subsribe, and are available on the web at
http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/ (under Introduction)
Please ignore the rest of this message if you are already aware of this.

Thanks!

 - Len Thomas
   distance-sampling list admin

Why shouldn't I send attachments?
---------------------------------

1. Remember that your message gets passed on to several hundred other people,
some of whom may not have high-speed access to the internet and others who
may not have mail spoolers with large capacities.  By sending a large
attachment without their prior consent, you risk crashing some people's mail
systems.

2. Many of the people on the list will not be interested in your particular
question, so will not want to see the dataset/screengrab you are posting.
This is frustrating for them if they spent many minutes downloading your
message down a 'phone line.

3. Many mail reading programs cannot deal with attachments, and your message
shows up on such systems as a seemingly random series of ASCII text.

What should I do instead?
-------------------------

1. If you have an anonymous ftp server at your site, upload your
picture/dataset to it (*zipped up* to make it more compact and easier to
transport) and include details of how to download the file inside your
*text only* message for those who are interested.

2. If you have a web server, the easiest thing for pictures is to put them on
your server and provide the URL (web address) in your message.

3. If you have none of these, offer to email the file to anyone who asks you
for it.  You will be surprised how few people do!  However, this way, you can
be sure that it will reach those who are interested.

These things take more time on your part, but people (such as me) will thank
you for your politeness!

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

             email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
   RUWPA home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk
Distance home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

messages.subject: Re: Cyprus mouflon
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kostas,

Firstly, I hope you won't send a large attachment to the list next time you
have a question!  (see my previous message).

> >In Cyprus we have an endemic species of wild sheep, the Cyprus mouflon
> >(Ovis gmelini ophion) that lives in the Paphos forest.  This forest (~
> >60000 ha) is in the SW part of the island.  The mouflon used to be very
> >abundant in the middle ages but due to intensive hunting it had reached
> >the brings of extinction in the 1930s.  Since then it is strictly
> >protected and the population has reached good numbers, estimated in a
> >few thousands.  In 1992 a brief helicopter survey was conducted and the
> >ppln was estimated between 900-1500 animals.  The growing damages that
> >the mouflon is causing in row crops, vineyards and orchards in areas
> >near the forest edge has led to the decision in counting the ppln in a
> >more accurate manner so that the right management decisions could be
> >taken.  In 1997 the Game Fund, the service responsible for wildlife
> >conservation in Cyprus has started a program counting the sheep.  We
> >have established 14 routes (lightly traveled forest roads) that run
> >through the mouflon habitat and cover most of the forest's valleys.

It is almost always a bad idea to use roads as transect routes.  They simply
not representative of the survey area you wish to cover.  For example, sheep
may be attracted by the vegetation that grows by roads.  Conversely they may
be scared off by the human presence along roads.  Roads tend to avoid steep
rocky areas where sheep may be more common, or less common.  etc etc etc.
The bottom line is that when your transect lines are not placed according to
some random (or systematic random) survey design there is always the danger
that your estimates contain a bias of unknown magnitude.  At the very least
you need to do some off-road transects to validate the roadside ones; better
still would be to think about how an off-road program could be initiated and
drop the roadside counts if possible.

> >Every route was traveled at least 2 times, some 3 times by the same
> >observers between September and January.   We have a 3-year data set
> >that we started analyzing using DISTANCE.
> >PROBLEMS:
> >1.  We plotted the frequency distribution of the right-angle distances
> >to get the probability density function.  The program chose the
> >half-normal-cosine model that gave us a ppln estimate of 3600 animals

I had a quick look at the Distance project file you enclosed and see the
following potential problems:

1. problems with the way the data is set up.
If you surveyed the same line many times within a year, it is fine to pool
the observations within lines, but you need to make sure you multiply the
effort up accordingly.  So, for example if your first trasect
is 11.5 kilometers long and you surveyed it 2 times that year,
the effort should be 2*11.5 = 23.  If you didn't do this, the population
estimate will be far to high.

2. problems with the data you collected.
A quick look at the histogram of distances reveals some potential problems.
(I put a copy in http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/images/mouflon.jpg if
anyone else is interested).  One problem is rounding - clearly your distances
are rounded to the nearest 50 meters.  This means you should group your data
before analysis (using Data Filter | Intervals).  More importantly, given
that you have 143 observations, you have far too few observations at 0
distance.  I suspect you have an evasive movement problem (see Distance
sampling book, pages 31-34 and elsewhere), which means you will underestimate
density.  Thirdly, your analysis didn't include any truncation, which is
important for robust estimation (see Distance sampling book again).  As a
first attempt at salvaging the data, I tried the intervals 0-75m, 75-175 and
175-275; however you'd need to do more thinking and discussing to see what's
best.  If you have an evasive movement problem, you definitely need to change
your field protocol.

All of this convinces me that you should either (1) (re-)read the Distance
Sampling book and/or (2) come on the workshop(s) that we are organizing this
summer (http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distanceworkshop/).

> >with a 33% CV!!  Then, we tried the uniform distribution with similar
> >ppln estimate but with a 22% CV.  We want to try to use the Fourier
> >Series model but the program does not allow to do so.  Also, it seems

Yes it does.  Fourier series is the Uniform + Cosine Adjustment.  Look at the
index of the Distance sampling book (available online at
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/) under Fourier series model and
you will see this referred to on pages 48 and 63-64.

> >that we cannot use our replications of each route in the program.

You can, as I outlined above.  You can also code your data in such a way as
to get estimates of density by year, but I dont' have time to discuss that
now.  I think it has been discussed previously (although I may be wrong
there) - see the distance-sampling list archives at
http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/

messages.subject: Re: Cyprus mouflon
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kostas,

Firstly, I hope you won't send a large attachment to the list next time you
have a question!  (see my previous message).

> >In Cyprus we have an endemic species of wild sheep, the Cyprus mouflon
> >(Ovis gmelini ophion) that lives in the Paphos forest.  This forest (~
> >60000 ha) is in the SW part of the island.  The mouflon used to be very
> >abundant in the middle ages but due to intensive hunting it had reached
> >the brings of extinction in the 1930s.  Since then it is strictly
> >protected and the population has reached good numbers, estimated in a
> >few thousands.  In 1992 a brief helicopter survey was conducted and the
> >ppln was estimated between 900-1500 animals.  The growing damages that
> >the mouflon is causing in row crops, vineyards and orchards in areas
> >near the forest edge has led to the decision in counting the ppln in a
> >more accurate manner so that the right management decisions could be
> >taken.  In 1997 the Game Fund, the service responsible for wildlife
> >conservation in Cyprus has started a program counting the sheep.  We
> >have established 14 routes (lightly traveled forest roads) that run
> >through the mouflon habitat and cover most of the forest's valleys.

It is almost always a bad idea to use roads as transect routes.  They simply
not representative of the survey area you wish to cover.  For example, sheep
may be attracted by the vegetation that grows by roads.  Conversely they may
be scared off by the human presence along roads.  Roads tend to avoid steep
rocky areas where sheep may be more common, or less common.  etc etc etc.
The bottom line is that when your transect lines are not placed according to
some random (or systematic random) survey design there is always the danger
that your estimates contain a bias of unknown magnitude.  At the very least
you need to do some off-road transects to validate the roadside ones; better
still would be to think about how an off-road program could be initiated and
drop the roadside counts if possible.

> >Every route was traveled at least 2 times, some 3 times by the same
> >observers between September and January.   We have a 3-year data set
> >that we started analyzing using DISTANCE.
> >PROBLEMS:
> >1.  We plotted the frequency distribution of the right-angle distances
> >to get the probability density function.  The program chose the
> >half-normal-cosine model that gave us a ppln estimate of 3600 animals

I had a quick look at the Distance project file you enclosed and see the
following potential problems:

1. problems with the way the data is set up.
If you surveyed the same line many times within a year, it is fine to pool
the observations within lines, but you need to make sure you multiply the
effort up accordingly.  So, for example if your first trasect
is 11.5 kilometers long and you surveyed it 2 times that year,
the effort should be 2*11.5 = 23.  If you didn't do this, the population
estimate will be far to high.

2. problems with the data you collected.
A quick look at the histogram of distances reveals some potential problems.
(I put a copy in http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/images/mouflon.jpg if
anyone else is interested).  One problem is rounding - clearly your distances
are rounded to the nearest 50 meters.  This means you should group your data
before analysis (using Data Filter | Intervals).  More importantly, given
that you have 143 observations, you have far too few observations at 0
distance.  I suspect you have an evasive movement problem (see Distance
sampling book, pages 31-34 and elsewhere), which means you will underestimate
density.  Thirdly, your analysis didn't include any truncation, which is
important for robust estimation (see Distance sampling book again).  As a
first attempt at salvaging the data, I tried the intervals 0-75m, 75-175 and
175-275; however you'd need to do more thinking and discussing to see what's
best.  If you have an evasive movement problem, you definitely need to change
your field protocol.

All of this convinces me that you should either (1) (re-)read the Distance
Sampling book and/or (2) come on the workshop(s) that we are organizing this
summer (http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distanceworkshop/).

> >with a 33% CV!!  Then, we tried the uniform distribution with similar
> >ppln estimate but with a 22% CV.  We want to try to use the Fourier
> >Series model but the program does not allow to do so.  Also, it seems

Yes it does.  Fourier series is the Uniform + Cosine Adjustment.  Look at the
index of the Distance sampling book (available online at
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/) under Fourier series model and
you will see this referred to on pages 48 and 63-64.

> >that we cannot use our replications of each route in the program.

You can, as I outlined above.  You can also code your data in such a way as
to get estimates of density by year, but I dont' have time to discuss that
now.  I think it has been discussed previously (although I may be wrong
there) - see the distance-sampling list archives at
http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/

> >Finally, once we put the data in we cannot edit anything in the AREA,
> >REGION section.
